findings.where: First screen, Mark's photograph (desktop and phone); the same keyed cut-out in the Texture 'Graded for the site' image and the motion-sketch preview card
findings.fault: The brief asked for a full-bleed photograph of Mark speaking. The page cuts him out of his backdrop and sets him on flat slate, so all that's left is a very large head and shoulders with a hard keyed edge round the hair and suit. The lectern, the room and the light are gone. It looks less like a photo of Mark at work and more like a cut-out pasted onto a coloured ground, and at this scale his face outweighs both his line and the action.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging the first screen first: v7's lever is Mark at work, with real people in real light. A development-bank visitor would object too, because a pasted-on head reads as cheap or slick, not as a senior advisor.

findings.where: Phone first screen, the photograph above the heading
findings.fault: The cut-out stops in a hard horizontal edge at the collar, just above the heading. Mark reads as a head floating on the navy ground, with the first line of type sitting right under the cut.
findings.who_objects: A phone visitor (often arriving from LinkedIn), for whom this is the first view of Mark. A severed-looking head undercuts the refined, serious tone the founder asked for.

findings.where: Article specimen, the blue numbers of the three-item list; the note beside it that reads 'Grey for reading, blue only where something can be clicked'
findings.fault: The list numbers are set in the link blue but can't be clicked. That breaks the page's own stated rule and makes them look like footnote or anchor links.
findings.who_objects: A reader of Mark's articles, who sees blue numbers and tries to click them. Angélique too: she is told blue means clickable and then sees it break in the first article.

findings.where: Article specimen, the 'Streamlining the PPP Process … Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF' row under the article
findings.fault: The row has no label and sits inside the article column between two hairlines, so it's unclear whether it's this article's attachment, a related talk or the start of a list. Its download arrow and 'PDF' label also promise a direct file download (its link actually goes to #article), where the house pattern is a PDF behind its own HTML page.
findings.who_objects: A bank officer looking for Mark's talks, who can't tell what the row is or whether they'll get a page or a file. The research calls the PDF list 'the product', and here it reads as an afterthought.

findings.where: Nav, desktop and phone: 'Profile', 'Articles and talks', 'Blog', and no 'Contact'
findings.fault: 'Articles and talks' and 'Blog' overlap: the specimen article is labelled 'Blog No. 8' but would just as well go under articles, so a visitor can't tell where a piece of writing lives. There is also no Contact item, so on any page other than the home hero, the only route to Mark is the address in the footer.
findings.who_objects: A visitor arriving deep on an article from a social post, who looks in the nav for how to reach Mark and finds nothing. The first-visit-trust rule asks for a 'Contact' label in the navigation.

findings.fault: This is a button (it does something on the page), but it's styled as a bold underlined blue link, which is the look the page keeps for navigation.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who reads it as a link to another page and doesn't expect it to replay the animation in place. It borrows a signifier from another function.

findings.fault: In the footer the logo leads and Mark's name shrinks to a small sans line beside the email at the far right. The hero gets this right (name first, logo beside it), and the footer reverses it.
findings.who_objects: The founder: 'his name leads, with the logo beside it' is one of the personal-advisor tests. On every article page the footer is the identity line, and it makes the firm the brand.

findings.where: First screen, the warm-white mark and wordmark on slate
findings.fault: A reversed (light) version of the logo has been made for the dark hero. The client holds only the full-colour logo, and a version he doesn't hold needs his yes first.
findings.who_objects: Mark, as owner of the logo. The brand-palette rule allows a new logo version only with the client's agreement.

findings.where: Nav, 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the logo
findings.fault: The name sits in the usual home-link spot, in the nav-link colour, but only the logo next to it actually links home.
findings.who_objects: A visitor on a deep page who clicks the name to go home and nothing happens. The logo beside it is a workaround.

findings.where: First screen, the 'Placeholder: Mark's photo…' caption (desktop bottom-left under the action; phone under the action, a whole screen below the photo)
findings.fault: The caption sits with the text column and the email action, not with the photograph it describes, so it reads as a note about the action.
findings.who_objects: The founder reviewing the tile, who has to work out which image the caption belongs to. It is a proximity fault.

findings.where: First screen heading, 'In my view, we are at a turning point…'
findings.fault: The second word in the largest type on the page is 'we'. On first read, a visitor can take it as the firm's 'we' before the sentence makes clear it means the whole PPP field.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test names a firm's 'we' as a fail. The display line is the one place it can't be misread.

findings.where: Article specimen, the 'Streamlining…' title and 'Lecture · 23 April 2026' line
findings.fault: The row's text is indented about 4 px from the left edge of the article column, so it sits just off the text above it on both desktop and phone.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, and the founder, who sees an edge that looks like it wasn't meant.

findings.fault: The heading uses a straight apostrophe, while the article body uses curly quotes (‘chapter topics’, ‘one-size-fits-all’).
findings.who_objects: A reader of a legal journal-style page, where mixed quote marks at display size look careless.

findings.where: Palette, the text-pair table at phone width
findings.fault: The ratio '11.66 : 1' breaks across two lines, leaving the '1' alone on the second line.
findings.who_objects: The founder reading the tile on a phone, who sees a broken figure.

findings.where: Type pair (desktop), the two description paragraphs
findings.fault: The two descriptions start at different heights: the Public Sans one sits well above the Newsreader one beside it, so the two columns don't line up.
findings.who_objects: The founder comparing the pair, for whom the uneven start reads as unfinished.
